content: An example of resource estimation was demonstrated through an evaluation of the costs associated with a public health surveillance system in Kentucky. This system actively solicited case reports of type A hepatitis. In 1983, the resources allocated for the direct operation of this system were primarily spent on personnel and telephone expenses, which were estimated at $3,764 and $535, respectively. The system identified nine additional cases that would not have been detected through a passive surveillance system. Furthermore, it was estimated that seven hepatitis cases were prevented by administering prophylaxis to the contacts of these nine case-patients. This method of resource assessment focuses solely on the personnel and material resources required for the operation of the surveillance system. It does not account for a broader definition of costs that might be included in a more comprehensive evaluation. The evaluation of the system's operational resources should not be conducted in isolation from the program or initiative that depends on the public health surveillance system. A more realistic approach for some surveillance systems might involve assessing costs relative to the system's objectives and usefulness. The evaluation design must be carefully focused to ensure that time and resources are utilized as efficiently as possible. This involves identifying the intended uses of the evaluation, specifying the questions it aims to answer, and determining standards for assessing the system's performance. Depending on the specific purpose of the evaluation, its design may range from straightforward to complex. An effective evaluation design requires a clear understanding of its purpose by all stakeholders and a commitment from those who need the findings to use the information generated. When multiple stakeholders are involved, agreements clarifying roles and responsibilities may need to be established among those implementing the evaluation. Standards for assessing the performance of the public health surveillance system define what the system must achieve to be considered successful in meeting its objectives. These standards specify, for example, the levels of usefulness and simplicity relevant to the system's goals. Useful standards for performance assessment can be developed through a review of current scientific literature on the health-related event under surveillance and/or consultation with appropriate specialists, including data users. To gather credible evidence regarding the performance of the surveillance system, it is essential to describe the actions taken as a result of analyzing and interpreting the data from the system. This includes characterizing the entities that have used the data to make decisions and take actions, as well as listing other anticipated uses of the data. The evidence collected should address the system's usefulness and the impact of its activities.
